Uniform Title: *Ṣaṭcakranirṇaya* Manuscript: BHU C4253 Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S.G. Dyczkowski.
Revision 0: April 7, 2012 Place of Publication: India Ṣaṭcakranirṇaya (The Determination of the Six Wheels)
Now, this Determination of the Six Chakras (Ṣaṭcakranirṇaya) is being written.
Oṃ! Those who do not know the body as having six wheels, sixteen supports, three targets, and five voids, are not fit for the Kula tradition. 1.
The wheel [of the body] extends as far as the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmabila*),
and from it the stalk of yoga has arisen throughout the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving.
It is called the Brahmakānda because it supports the root of Brahman and bestows the bliss of Brahman.
This is the intention of other treatises.
The triad of channels is taught therein, where consciousness dissolves; that is also known by the synonym "kanda," and it is remembered as the "aperture of Brahmā."
The channels on the left and right are known as *viḍā* and *piṅgalā*;
situated between them is the central channel, remembered as *suṣumṇā*. (Folio 193 is missing, but this appears to be a numbering error for page 194a.)
The channel known as Brahmanāḍī clearly reveals Brahman;
its bulbous root (kanda) is said to be located one finger-breadth above and below the navel.
That should be known as a triangle, three fingers in width;
situated in its center is the Śakti, the devourer of the five causes.
Through the practice of contraction, she becomes awakened;
she is to be reached through both existence and non-existence, having gone to the supreme state.
Knowing this, O highly fortunate one, establish yourself in the foundation of the bulb (kandādhāra);
remaining there, one should abandon one's own material form.

One should cause [the disciple] to grasp Śiva, who has reached the state of meditative cultivation, who is all-pervading, and by attaining whom one crosses to the further shore of the terrible ocean of saṃsāra. (9)
The second, however, is the navel-cakra, resembling the earring of a serpent;
it is renowned for its coiled form and is the cause of rising and setting.
This is the intended meaning of other treatises.
The Śakti resides in the center of the navel, having the form of a sleeping serpent;
it is endowed with five hoods, spirals to the left, and consists of three coils.
The fifty-fold mother of the twice-born, known as Praṇava, she who moves through the three vehicles,
ascending and descending in sequential union, is the auspicious one who nourishes Śiva until the end.
When awakened, it should be known as subtle; when asleep, it is in the form of a coil.
Measuring fifteen finger-breadths in width and possessing immeasurable color, it is the fire-drill of the Kula.
When he is situated in its center with a one-pointed mind,
O beloved, he sees various kinds of signs like those in a dream.
Therefore, with every effort, one should awaken the Lord in the form of a coil;
the third wheel in the heart, which pervades the thirty-six [principles], is like a ruby in appearance and possesses a brilliance equal to the sun. (16)
Herein is an example.
Six finger-breadths above the navel and six finger-breadths above the throat, one should know that to be the heart, the great abode of the universe. (17)
In the center of the heart-wheel is a lotus measuring sixteen finger-breadths across,
eight finger-breadths in length, hanging with its face turned downwards.
Indeed, the very footprint of a swan is endowed with a pericarp and filaments;
there, the yogi who has attained practice beholds the Self by means of the self.
The fourth is the Kaṇḍacakra, which is the domain where the channels meet;
it is declared to be the heart, the junction of all the channels.
This is the intention of other treatises.
From the form of the throat, hunger and thirst [arise].
Even when the tongue is slightly placed upon the root of the palate and the lower lip of the pure twice-born is opened,
by drinking even a slight flow of nectar from the moon, there is the cessation of hunger, thirst, death, burning fever, and disease.
The fifth is the Bindu-cakra, which consists of three segments and has the sky as its domain;
it is beyond the sky, supremely peaceful, and established as the very form of the Self.
Situated between the eyebrows is the wheel called Bindu, which bestows liberation;
it is the deity who possesses five colors and is endowed with the five times.
Constantly endowed with five times ten thousand [beats], yet devoid of five by five;
it is free from conceptual proliferation, without appearance, and measured by the size of a single thumb.
The sixth is indeed the palate-cakra, difficult to attain even for the gods;
one should meditate upon it as having a luster equal to the moon, endowed with a digit (kalā). (25)
An illustration of this is as follows:
In the center of the palate is the wheel (cakra) endowed with the digit known as Amṛtā;
there indeed resides the Supreme Lord, the wielder of the staff (Daṇḍapāṇi). (26)
Measuring three finger-breadths, it has a triangular shape;
from the twice-born caste down to the lowest caste, she is of a single uniform form.
Above that is the Cakrāsana wheel, devoid of lines and openings; it is beyond measurement and form, to be realized through meditative contemplation, and eternally manifest.
Where that stainless power, devoid of form, resides,
she always finds rest together with Śiva in one place.
Above the letter *ha*, one should place the city of the path of Kālāgni.
For they have indeed reached dissolution in the All-Supporting One, who is the foundation of the ankles and knees. || 30 ||
O beautiful lady, everything [is placed] in the contraction within the contraction, in the fourth corner;
from the fourth corner it goes to the one called Birth, and from there to Skanda.

From the *skanda* [cakra], within the pot-like interior of that which is called *kuṇḍalī* in the center of *kuṇḍalī*, that indeed is the place of animation for all beings, situated within the sheath of the individual soul (*jīva*). (32)
From Sañjīvanī it goes to Kūrma, from Kūrma to Sparśa-saṃjñaka;
from Sparśa to the root of Lalanā, and likewise from the one called Lālā to Lambaka. || 33 ||
Thus, these sixteen channels are established in the midst of the family (kula). || 34 ||

Having pierced through these, the power (śakti) should proceed to the external position along with the quarter-step (sapāda-śampada). That power known as Ūhaka, which descends through the support (ādhāra) toward the lower path—
its sixteen streams (dhārāḥ) should be performed at the end.
In the foundation of all, known as the *nūta* [or *bhūta*], there is the synonym for the anus:
*Kālāgnirudra*.
The contraction of desire (*kāmasaṅkoca*) is the vital air (*vāyu*) of this very [organ].
The two paths of the *yoni* are always situated at the junction of the vital winds;
by bringing them to a state of equilibrium through the power of the *aśakti*, the divine battle proceeds.

Having called out to that anus, which is the support of all and the [place for] the fingers... above which is the four-cornered [region], the quadrangular place called "birth" (*janma*) located in the penis; it is at this place that, during the time of union between woman and man, the seed falls and becomes the embryo. Within the interior of the golden [receptacle] is what is called "birth."
In the animal realm, it is six finger-breadths; in the upward movement, it is two finger-breadths.
This is the intention of other treatises.
In the syllable *ja* there is birth, and in the syllable *ma* there is death;
that which is the locus of the fear of birth and death, the wise know that to be the place of birth.
Two finger-breadths above the penis is the *janmakanda*;
two finger-breadths above that is a triangle, which is the support for the three channels (*nāḍī*).
For instance, they know that the base of the penis is seen one finger-breadth below the channels.
Therein, in the center, is the great wheel known as the bulb (kanda);
its designation is the palate, and its purification is according to its name.
This is the intention of another treatise.
The region between the navel and the penis is proclaimed as the *kanda*, the support of the principles (*tattva*).
Within it, situated in the center of the fire, is consciousness devoid of the ordinary mind;
it is six-spoked, throbbing, and established within the location of the *kanda*.
It is known as Kulabindu, and likewise it is known as Brahmabila.
This is called the "excellent" (*prakṛṣṭaka*).
Kuṇḍalinī is in the region of the navel; the "belly of the jar" (ghaṭodara) is situated within the lotus of the heart at the center of the navel, and its synonym is *sañjīvanī*.
It is the midpoint of the cavity formed by the lotuses of the navel and the heart.
The tortoise is the heart; that place where all objects abide like the limbs of a tortoise is the "tortoise-support," which is the entire sky.
Four finger-breadths from the heart is the place called *lola*; *lolā* means the tongue, and its root is the *lolāmūla*.
The location is the throat. Six finger-breadths below the *lampikā* is that which is called *lambā*;
below *lambā* is *ghaṇṭikā*, and the "mouth of the guru" (*guruvaktra*)—the "mouth of the guru" being designated as the *bindu*.

The "middle of the eyebrows" (bhrūmadhya) refers to the point known as the *bindu* located in the station of the fourth state (*turya*), which is described as "all. It is the face of the Unborn, the space that is unborn; because birth does not exist therein, it is called the "banner" (*dhvaja*) in that station.
Thus, what is the "sixteenfold basis"?
Now, the three hundred thousand [recitations].
The internal target, the external target, and the target free from both;
by means of the external application, there is the movement of the image and so forth—
[this practice] is endowed with all limbs and united with the meaning of all tantras.
Having attained the state of consciousness through the union of mind and its functions,
the vision of the inner goal proceeds toward the supreme.
That state which belongs to one established in their own place, having cast both the internal and external out, is the vision of the inner target.

That which is called the "middle" is that in which one perceives nothing at all; it is free from the three marks (*lakṣa*), transcendent, and immutable. Existing in all states yet not being a state itself—that is said to be the supreme mark.
This is called the "pentad of space."
First is the Brahma-void; the second is the Viṣṇu-void; the third is the Rudra-void; the fourth is called the Īśvara-void;
and Sadāśiva is the fifth—this indeed is the pentad of voids.

O Dear One, those who know the knowledge of Brahman understand that from the navel up to the heart is the supreme earthly principle (*pārthiva-tattva*), by virtue of its waking state activity. From the heart to the location of the throat is proclaimed as the station of Viṣṇu.
They know that the region from the throat up to the middle of the eyebrows is the station of Rudra.
The fire-principle (tejas-tattva) remains established in the state of deep sleep;
however, within the Bindu, there exists the sequence known as Īśvara, extending up to the level of Tālvan.
The object of knowledge is to be known as resting in the fourth state (turyāvasthā) and supported by the element of air (vāyutatva);
the station of Sadāśiva extends from the end of the palate to the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta). || 5 ||
Established in the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), it is like the sky— [text missing]— or joined with the sixth [vowel], transparent and free from the conceit of "I. (3)
It is endowed with *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *vaṣaṭ*;
it is joined with long vowels, and is the *haṃsa* adorned by the limbs of the *haṃsa*.
The Lord, conjoined with the Śakti-mantra, abides in the state of supreme bliss;
together with Vyāpinī, he is the Lord of Vyāpinī, the creator of emanation.
Situated within the thirty-six principles, he is the supreme embodiment of mantra;
yet he transcends mantra, being the ultimate peace, the end of the state of Unmanī, and free from all affliction.
It is known as the abode of the abodes of all luminaries, the illuminator of consciousness and bliss,
accessible solely through the knowledge of the intellect, and beyond the range of others.
He is beyond the state of the supreme self, devoid of [all attributes],
auspicious, omnipresent, void, and situated both outside and within.
Folios 200–239 appear to be missing due to a numbering error. (p.
240a) [He is] the eternally risen, great splendor, the Sun-Swan whose nature is Śiva;
the God situated within the wheel of the zodiac, established in the two solstices. || 9 ||
In the right side of the belly is the Moon, and in the left is the Sun;
joined with both fortnights, it resides within all beings.
The Lord of Yoga, attainable through Yoga, transcending Yoga, free from all affliction;
the sixfold path, yet beyond the sixfold path, the Void endowed with the six. || 11 ||

Situated in the center of the heart-lotus, concealed from the grasped and the grasper, he is the Lord of Consciousness whose nature is sentience, possessing six paths and known as the six states of being. (12)

The nature of space, moving in space, abiding in space, beyond space, the lord of space, and the one who goes in space; the support of the banks [of the river of existence], the non-family (Akula), and the one who brings about the family (Kula).
I bow to that Supreme Lord, whom they call the kinsman, the mother, the father, the friend, and the teacher, and who is said to be one's entire possession. (14)
Salutation to that Perfect Self, who possesses omniscience, the attainment of knowledge, independence of consciousness, and unimpeded power. 15.
Salutation to that Self who is all-pervading, whose pervasiveness is unique due to the relinquishment of all senses, and who is endowed with the qualities of the sixfold attributes. 16.
Salutations to that eternal Self, who is endowed with qualities such as knowledge, who is devoid of the material qualities (guṇas), and in whom neither decay nor birth exists.
Salutation to that whose nature is emptiness, which has neither root nor tip, nor the cardinal directions nor the intermediate directions, nor sound, nor likewise space.
Or [is it that] one who is eyeless sees, one who is tongueless tastes flavor, and one who is earless hears? Homage to that wondrous Self! (19)
Salutation to that Self who is the Creator, who is devoid of any cause for the universe. || 20 ||
Just as time, though devoid of threads, accomplishes its work, even so is the eternal agent; salutation to that Self who is the agent. 21.
Salutation to that Self of Stability, who dwells eternally in the body, established in the midst of the universe, having attained the form of steadfastness. || 22 ||
Salutation to that Self in the form of Time, who is called the one Haṃsa-Kāla by whom this entire universe is withdrawn and who remains as the absolute Self alone.
Salutation to that one whose nature is *māyā*, who dwells as many forms within this world of moving and non-moving beings, and who, having withdrawn this universe, becomes one again. 24.

Salutation to that one whose nature is the Hero (vīrātman), by whom the entire universe, endowed with its essential principles, is held at the tip of his finger of knowledge and is whirled about with ease. || 25 ||
Salutations to that gross-bodied one, within whose center the entire universe is seen as a mere mustard seed, and who likewise contains the universe. 26.
Salutation to that subtle Self, of whom this world is said to be but a hundredth or even a thousandth part of the tip of a hair.
Salutation to that Self of the field, who is the great locus within the body, presided over by all sentient beings, and the manifestation of the cage of sentient beings. 28.

Salutations to that Kṣetrātman (the Self of the Field), who is the Knower of the Field, whose nature is light, who is established in the center of the heart, who is pure, stainless, and the Haṃsa. || 29 ||
Salutation to that Self of Knowledge, who is radiant as the Unmanifest (unmanī) on the far shore of great darkness; knowing whom, there is no further rebirth. (30)
Since the effect is indeed attained through knowledge as its superior cause, and since satisfaction is all-pervading—to that Self of Knowledge, obeisance! (31)
Salutation to that Self of Life (jīvātman), who, abiding within the body, revolves in the navel-cakra and pervades the heart as the light of consciousness. || 32 ||
Salutation to that one whose nature is the *haṃsa*, who sports between those two—the *iḍā*, the greatly meritorious Gaṅgā, and the *suṣumṇā*, the Yamunā. (33)
Salutation to that Pure Self, who is pure in the bright fortnight, who abides in the white waters of the Gaṅgā, and who is ever devoted to white (pure) deeds. || 34 ||
Salutation to that Kṛṣṇa-ātman, who is dark, who dwells in the waters of the Yamunā during the dark fortnight, and who is eternally devoted to cruel deeds. || 35 ||
O you who always carry away [the breath] with the *reca* [exhalation], you who are greedy for the taste of the six flavors—to that Sun-self who eternally blazes with heat, I bow. (36)
Salutation to that one whose nature is Soma, who dwells in the *pūraka* [breathing] at night as the essence of nectar, and who is eternally the cause of nourishment. || 37 ||
Salutations to that one whose self is fire, who, being himself satisfied, satisfies the gods established on the path of the gods and the ancestors in the abode of the ancestors.
During a solar eclipse, he who is conjoined with the equinox is dissolved within the heart, between the iḍā and piṅgalā channels.
Salutation to that one whose essence is the sacred ford, through whom merit is gained by offerings to the gods and ancestors. || 40 ||

Salutation to that Self of the Ascendant (lagnātman), who, at the rising of the moon, through the movement of the moon, bestows the excellence of all undertakings upon the portion of the *iḍā* when it is joined with the *piṅgalā*. 41.
Salutation to that which is the essence of the place, where, in the auspicious field at the end of the twelve, there occurs an eclipse of the sun of consciousness, accompanied by Śiva-Rāhu. (42)
Salutation to that one whose nature is mantra, wherein indeed the moon known as apāna resides, wherein the sun has set, and wherein there is the cessation of both prāṇa and apāna. || 43 ||
Salutations to that worshipful Self, who is worshipped by yogis through the rite of offering to Brahman as day and night come to their end.
Salutation to that Japātman (the Self of Recitation), who, as Śiva abiding within one's own body, utters [the mantra] himself and bestows liberation at the end of the body's life.
Salutation to that Hotṛ-self, wherein consciousness is the sacrificial field, the mind is the Hotṛ-priest, the supreme extraction is called immortality, and the mantra is known as the syllable "Ha."
Salutation to that Self who is the Eater, the God who abides within all gods, the seven-flamed Supreme Lord, who consumes food containing the six tastes within himself.
Salutation to that one whose essence is light, who, possessing great splendor, eternally and perfectly illuminates everything both external and internal with his rays. (48)
Salutation to that one whose self is space, who, having transcended the elemental ether, is the supreme Brahman of space, the stainless radiance of consciousness. 49.
Salutations to that Soul of Yoga, whom those who have conquered sleep through great awakening, who are disciplined and whose senses are restrained, perceive as the light of lights.
Salutation to that Prāṇātman, who is Brahmā during inhalation (pūraka), Viṣṇu during retention (kumbhaka), and Rudra who dwells within exhalation (recaka).
In the state of Brahmā he creates the universe; in the state of Viṣṇu he is the one who effects its maintenance;
in the state of Rudra he indeed withdraws it—salutation to him whose nature is that of the sustainer.
Salutations to that one whose essence is mantra, by whom [the deity] endowed with the five measures and the five deities of grace is invoked here through the mantra. (53)

Salutation to Him whose nature is the [social] classes (varṇa), who moves by Himself, whose mode of subsistence is subtle, whose form is like a plow, who is beyond the unstruck sound (anāhata), and who is supremely peaceful.
Salutation to that Self who is the binder, by whom the ordinary accumulation of worlds is strung together like a garland with the snares consisting of merit and demerit.
Salutation to that Self of liberation, who is beyond all paths of the forest of existence, who is established in silence, who is beyond all that can be described, and who is supremely peaceful. (56)
Salutation to that Liṅga-soul, whose seat is this universe, whose form consists of space, and into whom all the principles (tattvas) dissolve. || 57 ||

Salutation to that Self of liberation, who is the end of the unmanifest state, supreme, pure, the reality of the *samanā* level, partless, and yet possessed of all parts through the pervasive power (*vyāpinī*).
Salutation to that Self of all, who is established in the midst of the universe among all things moving and unmoving, and who abides within the ocean of Māyā. || 59 ||
This divine hymn, equal to the best of praises, is an imperishable collyrium of knowledge;
it is remembered as that which opens the eyes of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance.
For men whose merit is exhausted, it immediately increases their righteousness;
it is supreme, pure, holy, and the remover of all suffering. (61)
The man who, knowing it to be complete with internal virtues, recites this,
shall have his soul purified of all sins and go to the eternal state.
